questions.title: Blushing is active hyperemia
questions.question: A 22-year-old second-year medical student develops a "red" face after being asked a question during lecture. Which of the following statements best describes this vascular reaction?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Oedema is fluid accumulation in the interstitial space, not the vascular reddening described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Petechial hemorrhage is a pinpoint bleed into the skin, not a reversible reddening from vasodilation.
explanations.C: Correct. Blushing results from arteriolar dilation increasing arterial inflow into facial skin, an active physiological process. This is the definition of active hyperemia. It is triggered here by an embarrassing moment, through sympathetic withdrawal and local vasodilator mechanisms, not by any pathological process.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acute congestion refers to impaired venous outflow, a passive process, not the arteriolar-dilation-driven active process of blushing.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Passive hyperemia (congestion) is caused by impaired venous outflow, not by increased arterial inflow as seen here.

questions.title: Post-fracture leg swelling is phlebothrombosis
questions.question: A 60-year-old woman sustained fractures of the right femur, pelvis, and left humerus in a motor vehicle collision. The fractures were stabilized, and the patient's recovery was uneventful. During a physical examination 3 weeks later, the physician observes swelling and warmth in the left leg, and there is local pain and tenderness in the left thigh. Which of the following processes is most likely occurring in the femoral vein?

explanations.A: Correct. Swelling, warmth, pain and tenderness in a limb weeks after immobilization from a fracture is the classic picture of phlebothrombosis -- thrombus formation in a non-inflamed deep vein. Immobilization promotes venous stasis, one arm of Virchow's triad, favouring clot formation in the stagnant femoral vein. This is the expected complication of prolonged bed rest after major fracture stabilization.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mural thrombosis describes a thrombus adherent to the wall of a chamber (typically cardiac), not the deep-vein process described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chronic passive congestion is a systemic pattern from right heart failure, not a localized limb finding from immobilization.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vegetations are thrombotic/infective masses on heart valves, unrelated to a limb-vein finding after fracture.

questions.title: Right heart failure causes chronic venous congestion
questions.question: Chronic general venous congestion is noticed in patients with:

explanations.A: Correct. Right-sided heart failure prevents the right heart from pumping venous return forward, so blood backs up throughout the systemic venous system. This produces chronic general (systemic) venous congestion, with findings such as hepatic and splenic congestion, dependent oedema and raised jugular venous pressure. This systemic, generalized pattern is what distinguishes right heart failure's effect from a localized cause of obstruction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Compression by a tumour causes localized, not general/systemic, venous obstruction confined to the drainage territory it compresses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Portal hypertension causes congestion specifically in the portal venous system (e.g. splenomegaly, oesophageal varices), not general systemic venous congestion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An enlarged lymph node compresses local venous or lymphatic drainage, not the systemic venous circulation as a whole.

questions.title: A detached venous thrombus embolises to the lung
questions.question: Detached non septic venous thrombus goes to the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brain is a destination for a systemic arterial embolus (e.g. from the left heart or a carotid plaque), not a venous one.
explanations.B: Correct. A thrombus that forms in the systemic venous circulation and detaches travels with venous blood flow back to the right heart and out into the pulmonary arterial circulation. It therefore lodges in the lung as a pulmonary embolus. This venous-to-pulmonary pathway is why the lung, not a systemic organ, is the destination of a detached venous thrombus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The kidney is a destination for a systemic arterial embolus, not a venous one, which is filtered by the lung first.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bone is not the typical destination of any embolus type described in this option set, venous or arterial.

questions.title: Phlebothrombosis forms in non-inflamed veins
questions.question: In phlebothrombosis the thrombus is formed in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A septic vein describes an infected vessel, not the defining site of phlebothrombosis.
explanations.B: Correct. Phlebothrombosis is thrombus formation specifically within a non-inflamed vein. This distinguishes it from thrombophlebitis, where the thrombus forms in a vein already inflamed. The name of the process (phlebothrombosis vs thrombophlebitis) tracks precisely this distinction in whether inflammation preceded the thrombus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inflamed veins are the site of thrombophlebitis, the counterpart process, not phlebothrombosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phlebothrombosis is, by its name and definition, a venous, not an arterial, process.

questions.title: Lines of Zahn are columns of platelets
questions.question: Lines of Zahn consist of:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the sole answer. Fibrin does accompany the platelet layers, but the named structural component of Lines of Zahn's pale bands is platelets.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Red blood cells form the alternating dark bands, not the pale bands that give Lines of Zahn their name.
explanations.C: Correct. Lines of Zahn are alternating pale and dark bands within a thrombus that formed in flowing blood during life. The pale bands correspond to layers of platelets, laid down in sequence as the thrombus builds up. This layered platelet structure is what distinguishes an antemortem thrombus from a postmortem clot, which lacks it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. White blood cells are not the named structural component of Lines of Zahn's alternating bands.

questions.hold: Printed key names 'clot' for a soft mass of blood constituents forming 'in stagnant blood inside the vessel during life' (Quiz 31 Q7: 'Soft mass of blood constituents in a stagnant blood inside the vessel during life called: ... The correct answer is: clot'). This contradicts the standard pathological distinction: a thrombus is defined as a solid mass forming from blood constituents within a vessel DURING LIFE, while a clot is coagulated blood forming after death (postmortem) or outside the vasculature -- the stem's own wording ('during life') is the textbook definition of thrombus, not clot. This is directly contradicted by this same quiz's own rows: Q2/Q5 (q246/q249) use 'thrombus'/'phlebothrombosis' for exactly this in-vessel-during-life process, Q6 (q250) describes Lines of Zahn as a feature of an antemortem (during-life) thrombus, and Q8 (q252) confirms Virchow's triad concerns 'thrombus' formation. Held per the printed-key-vs-pathology-vocabulary conflict rule (same handling as Q19, Q25, Q47, Q166, Q204, Q224, Q238 in this lane's earlier clusters), not resolved by inference.

questions.title: Virchow's triad concerns thrombus formation
questions.question: Virchow's triad is concerned with the formation of:

explanations.A: Correct. Virchow's triad names the three broad categories of factors that predispose to thrombus formation: endothelial injury, stasis or turbulence of blood flow, and hypercoagulability of the blood. It is specifically a framework for explaining why a thrombus forms, not for embolism or hemorrhage. This is why thrombus, and not the other options here, is the target concept of the triad.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ecchymosis is a bruise -- extravasated blood in the skin/subcutaneous tissue -- not explained by Virchow's triad's risk factors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An embolus is a thrombus fragment (or other material) that has already detached and travelled; Virchow's triad explains the initial thrombus formation, not the subsequent embolic event.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A haematoma is a localized collection of extravasated blood, not the intravascular thrombus formation Virchow's triad addresses.
